" is now most often used for the cute-only version, which keeps the kawaii imagery, such as Sanrio mascots, moe anime characters, frills, and pastel colors, along with falling pastel stars, kaomoji, pixel art, medical imagery, and bedrooms filled with plushies and anime figures. "

c: The word "Cutecore" existed before the aesthetic, though its use was niche. An Everskies post on the subject says it appeared in the early 2010s as short for "cute but hardcore" and named music that mixed hardcore with kawaii elements, such as anime girls talking over the track or bloody anime girls on the cover art. YouTube content creator Addy Harajuku describes the same early use of the term for a hardcore subgenre that combined aggressive metal instrumentation or vocals with J-pop melodies and cutesy sound clips, comparable to the

, an electronic music microgenre originating from 4chan in the late 2000s, often used similar collages of "moe" anime characters, edgy humor, and blood splatters for its album art, which can be considered a loose stylistic precedent to later Cutecore edits.

The term was popularized in 2020 by a Tumblr user (who has requested anonymity and won't be named in this article) who posted photos of a cute bedroom with a dark, gloomy mood, featuring Sanrio plushies and other

, as well as fast food packaging like McDonald's Happy Meal boxes. A fan-run Tumblr archive of their posts credits them with inventing the style, and includes a reposted Q&A in which they say they mostly bought discontinued Sanrio items secondhand. One image from this period shows a Sanrio bedspread digitally edited to have bloody handprints.
Cutecore and Cutegore originally named the same community, one closer to
, in which blood, fake gore, and dark shadowy figures reminiscent of

appeared throughout. On the TikTok community, the two names have since separated, and that "Cutecore" now stands for kawaii culture while Cutegore continues as its own community. Another reason people switched from "Cutegore" to "Cutecore" is because the word "gore" could get accounts shadowbanned on Tumblr and Twitter.

As of October 2026, the #cutecore tag on TikTok mostly shows posts without blood or horror elements, such as pink Sanrio bedrooms, pixel art, and kaomoji. The #cutegore tag holds most of the horror-inspired content, along with some cute-only posts. Some TikTok users also prefer calling the non-gory version of the aesthetic "Kawaii Kei," although it is a Japanese-inspired Western moniker (treating "
" as equivalent to cute and "kei," meaning type, as equivalent to "core") rather than using authentic Japanese terminology.

c: Cutecore rooms range from slightly disorganized bedrooms evoking a "NEET" archetype to carefully arranged spaces with maximalist merchandise collection displays. Many have a "character shrine," where large collections of plushies (such as
) and anime figures (from IP franchises such as

, etc.) are packed onto shelves or beds. Characters like My Melody and Rilakkuma are often repeated across the display. Rooms in the Cutecore tag on TikTok are mostly bright and pink, while rooms in the Cutegore tag are shown in darker or more desaturated lighting, and may have horror posters (such as
), a silhouette, or a pixelated black figure edited in. The Tumblr user credited with starting the aesthetic often used dim lighting.

Pink is the dominant color, ranging from very light pastels to hot pink, often accented with white or strawberry red. Pink LED strips and filtered natural light are common and give the room a hazy glow that softens the clutter.
Bedding usually includes ruffled duvet covers, character-themed blankets, and many decorative pillows, such as strawberry-shaped ones. On the walls, posters and tapestries featuring
anime characters can be seen. The density of objects can make a room feel claustrophobic.

c: Edits in both forms start from cute subjects, usually
anime characters or plush toys. Cutegore edits add signs of physical harm, including bandages, eyepatches, and splattered fluids. Unlike

, which often features stylized or cartoonish gore such as eyeballs, Cutegore edits often use photorealistic textures of blood, bruising, or medical gauze overlaid on soft, childlike imagery. Cutecore edits without gore decorate the same kinds of subjects with kawaii digital stickers instead. These are also common in Cutegore, and include Sanrio characters, kaomoji, caramel pudding, cake, pastel rainbows (usually pink, yellow, and blue), 2000s technology such as the Nintendo DS, strawberries common in stationery from the
era, and falling stars in pastel colors.

Many edits are processed to look degraded, using noise, heavy JPEG compression, and pixelation that resemble 2000s web images or flip-phone photos. Consoles from this era, such as the Nintendo DS, Dreamcast, or Game Boy Advance, often appear as props.

Discarded fast food packaging, specifically from McDonald's (Happy Meal boxes) and strawberry milk cartons, also sometimes appears in these interiors, a motif popularized by the aesthetic's originator on Tumblr. It is associated with childhood comfort food and with the executive dysfunction linked to the NEET lifestyle, such as not cooking or doing other self-care tasks.

Backgrounds in Cutegore edits often show the cluttered interiors associated with the "NEET" (Not in Education, Employment, or Training) lifestyle. These spaces typically have unmade beds, piles of laundry, and rooms darkened by blackout curtains and lit only by computer screens or televisions. More extreme interpretations of the Cutegore aesthetic may place a stronger emphasis on graphic gore, such as objects resembling meat, like red-dyed instant noodles, and feature shadowy figures or creepy uncanny valley faces.

c: Usernames, video titles, captions, and playlist names in the aesthetic are often written with a lot of kaomoji (Japanese emoticons) and Unicode symbols (ASCII art). The kaomoji are often elaborate and show nervous, shy, or confused expressions, such as ( ꩜ ᯅ ꩜;) and (>_<). Text is often framed with decorative Unicode borders such as ୨୧ and ︶꒷, and written in Unicode fonts that imitate handwriting or "cutesy" script, which can make it hard to read.

A small set of emoji recurs. The pudding emoji (🍮) is extremely common and often acts as a reference to the Sanrio character Pompompurin. The ribbon (🎀) and strawberry (🍓) are also common, along with the bandage and syringe (🩹/💉), which come from Menhera medical imagery, or the bone (🦴), which can either tie into innocent themes of pets or Cutegore's emphasis on creepiness. Some combinations pair these with knives, guns, and blood drops, particularly in Cutegore. Small symbols such as ˚, ⋆, and ｡ are scattered around text, which adds visual clutter similar to that in the room photos.

c: Cutecore fashion interprets Japanese street styles through a Western and internet-centric lens. It borrows heavily from
(Japanese children's clothing) but recontextualizes it for an older demographic.

The silhouette typically consists of layered garments, including oversized knits, tiered mini-skirts, and leg warmers worn over patterned tights. Footwear focuses on heavy, chunky platforms from brands like Demonia or New Rock to ground the otherwise soft outfit. The Cutegore version of the aesthetic often juxtaposed those same clothes with darker elements, such as shirts from metal bands in a color palette black and red.

Specific Japanese children's brands from the early 2000s, such as Angel Blue, Mezzo Piano, and Daisy Lovers, are highly valued within the community. These garments are often sourced via resale markets, leading to high price inflation. The makeup style emulates a sickly or doll-like appearance, utilizing heavy blush placed high on the cheeks (similar to Byojaku), downturned eyeliner, and circle lenses to exaggerate eye size.

Criticism of Cutecore comes from several perspectives: former and current members describing their experiences in the community, creators making video essays about it, and writers objecting to particular imagery. Some of it applies to the whole community and some only to Cutegore. Several of the critics also say that most people who enjoy the aesthetic mean no harm and that many members are kind and supportive.
Cutecore has been criticized for taking the most popular, surface-level parts of Japanese
culture and leaving out its history. Critics say the version of Cutecore now in circulation amounts to a narrower kawaii culture, and that this gives a warped and appropriative picture of Japan.

The word "kawaii" has been disputed on its own. In 2021, a TikTok user who posted a cosplay video received comments claiming that non-Japanese people using the word was cultural appropriation and a slur. Harajuku model Haruka Kurebayashi responded that anyone can use the word "kawaii" regardless of nationality, gender, age, or skin color.
Some also believe that divorcing Cutecore from its
-inspired origins ("Cutegore") renders the label redundant to

. For example, Addy Harajuku argues that Cutecore does not need to exist, since its elements already appear in other kawaii and J-fashion styles. However, she does not think it should be condemned, and says it gives many young people their first route into kawaii pop culture,
Cutegore has been criticized for romanticizing gore in ways that go beyond mere fictional violence or cartoonish blood splatters. Critics such as one Everskies blogger separate this from enjoying
films, saying a horror viewer is not thinking about how cute the blood looks. They acknowledge that some users combine childlike imagery with horror as a way of coping, similar to

, but argue that heavy or real gore can retraumatize people and make their symptoms worse. In some fringe cases, real-life gore has appeared on Cutegore art, and one critic calls the use of crime scene photographs of real victims morally reprehensible, in contrast to medical photographs or fictional horror, which she says are neutral. One Everskies writer objects to what she describes as Cutegore's focus on covering Japanese people, especially women, whether real or fictional, in blood and injuries, and says it romanticizes violence toward Asians.

Addy describes the community as one with many vulnerable young people, and says that edgy, offensive humor and self-deprecation spread intolerance among them. She says Cutecore at times references lolicon media (such as

media with canonically adult characters, and that the style treats the former as standard practice. In her account, some teenagers post suggestive images of themselves and infantilize themselves without realizing it, and the spaces become less safe because content made by minors can be circulated and predatory users get chances to manipulate vulnerable members.

Some anti-terrorism researchers have described Cutecore as a gateway to grooming. Researcher Marc-André Argentino, who studies online radicalization, has analyzed how the aesthetic is weaponized within the "

," an extremist ecosystem where cutecore's pastel, seemingly innocent appearance camouflages content related to self-harm, eating disorders, and exploitation. Argentino identifies a gendered grooming dynamic where "

" adopting cutecore aesthetics are used to normalize harmful behaviors and recruit younger users, often escalating to real-world violence. However, this is an extremist appropriation of the aesthetic rather than an inherent feature of the entire cutecore community.

The Cutecore community faced backlash due to its cost-prohibitive barrier to entry, as well as the fact that consumer products and clothes associated with the aesthetic have their prices inflated by resellers, colloquially referred to as the "cutecore tax." A YouTuber who left the community describes feeling pressure to own wardrobes of Mezzo Piano and Mother Garden clothing and rooms full of My Melody and rare items in order to belong, and being called "broke" because she could not afford the clothes. She says that in late 2024 people shamed others for carrying an off-brand Mother Garden bag from Amazon and encouraged them to buy Randoseru instead, which she puts at $200 to $1,000. Overpricing and price gouging on platforms like Depop, Mercari Japan, and eBay have made secondhand items hard to find, and that people shame others for buying fast fashion or counterfeit anime figures while the secondhand route is out of reach. She also describes users comparing their rooms to others and feeling theirs are not cute enough.
People drawn to the aesthetic often have to deal with unrealistic beauty standards and self-comparison.

brands like Mezzo Piano and Angel Blue make children's clothing, and as such, they run very small. Because these clothes were originally intended for children, the pressure to fit into them leads to body shaming and the normalization of eating disorders. An ex-member of the cutecore fandom says that when she joined, she felt too big for it, even though her doctor had told her she was a healthy weight, and that she tried to lose more weight than she needed to. She says she saw many thin people who fit the clothes on Pinterest.
